question: On 4 October 2023 the Commission brought forward a proposal for a revised Animal Welfare Act1. However, the proposal does not include a ban on the breeding of pets with the aim of obtaining specific external characteristics which are harmful to the animal. Nor does it ban the import of such pets.

This is despite the fact that such breeding causes chronic and painful suffering to the animal, and that countries including the Netherlands and Norway have brought in national bans on the breeding of flat-faced dogs.

On 18 January 2024, the Danish Minister for Food, Agriculture and Fisheries stated in the Danish Parliament2 that a Member State cannot bring in a national ban on importing inbred animals, as this is at odds with EU rules on the free movement of goods. A national ban on inbreeding would have little effect if it could be circumvented by imports from other Member States where such breeding is authorised. 1.
Is the Commission planning to bring forward a ban on the breeding of pets with the aim of obtaining specific external characteristics that could subject the animals concerned to painful suffering?
Can an EU Member State impose a national import ban on inbred animals without such a ban infringing EU internal market trade rules?

Commission proposal on the welfare and traceability of dogs and cats https://www.ft.dk/aktuelt/webtv/video/20231/salen/46.aspx# – Point 8: 1st reading of B 47: Ban on the import and breeding of flat-faced dogs and dogs with unnaturally small skulls.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.4.2024) On 7 December 2023 the Commission adopted a proposal for a Regulation on the welfare of dogs and cats and their traceability1. The proposal has entered the ordinary legislative procedure and the co-legislators will shape the provisions before its adoption.

Article 6(3) of that proposal introduces an obligation on operators of breeding establishments to ensure that breeding strategies do not result in genotypes and phenotypes that have detrimental effects on the welfare of the dogs and cats, or of their descendants.

Also, in the management of the reproduction of dogs and cats by operators, the mating between parents and offspring, or between grandparents and grandchildren, is prohibited. Paragraph 4 of the same article empowers the Commission to establish specific criteria to be met by operators when designing breeding strategies to comply with the requirements of paragraph 3.

Article 25 of that proposal sets out the conditions under which Member States may maintain or adopt stricter national measures to protect the welfare of dogs and cats with regard to certain welfare areas. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of the said article stipulate that those rules must be compatible with the smooth functioning of the internal market.
Whether specific national measures comply with these preconditions needs to be answered on a case-by-case basis.
